steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a Gaussian process solver for PDEs with high-frequency and multi-scale solutions. Set up the PINN approach and why it struggles with high frequencies, then introduce our GP method and list the contributions (model, algorithm, results).

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Many scientific and engineering problems require us to solve a set of partial differential equations (PDEs). Machine learning (ML) solvers have recently got a lot of attention. Compared to traditional numerical methods, ML solvers don't need complex mesh designs and sophisticated numerical tricks, they are simple to implement, and they can solve inverse problems efficiently and conveniently. The most popular ML solver is the physics-informed neural network (PINN). Consider a PDE of the following general form,

where {\mathcal{F}} is the differential operator, \Omega is the domain, and \partial\Omega is the boundary of the domain. The PINN uses a deep neural network (NN) {\widehat{u}}_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\bf x}) to model the solution u. It samples N_{c} collocation points \{{\bf x}_{c}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{c}} from \Omega and N_{b} points \{{\bf x}_{b}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{b}} from \partial\Omega, and then minimizes a loss,

where L_{b}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{N_{b}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{b}}\left({\widehat{u}}_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\bf x}_{b}^{j})-g({\bf x}_{b}^{j})\right)^{2} is the boundary term that fits the boundary condition, and L_{r}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{N_{c}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{c}}\left({\mathcal{F}}[{\widehat{u}}_{{\bm{\theta}}}]({\bf x}_{c}^{j})-f({\bf x}_{c}^{j})\right)^{2} is the residual term that fits the equation.

The PINN has many success stories, but it often has a hard time solving PDEs whose solutions have high-frequency and multi-scale components. This agrees with the “spectrum bias” that has been observed in NN training. NNs can usually learn the low-frequency information efficiently, but learning the high-frequency knowledge is much harder. To alleviate this, recent work constructs a set of random Fourier features from zero-mean Gaussian distributions, and these random features are fed into the PINN layers for training (see (2)). This is effective, but the performance of the method is unstable, and it is very sensitive to the number and scales of the Gaussian variances, which are hard to choose beforehand.

- GP-HM
  - alternative arising ML solver framework: GPs
  - GP-HM = GP solver for High frequency and Multi-scale PDEs
  - Wiener-Khinchin theorem: model solution in frequency domain, estimate target frequencies from covariance function
  - efficient learning algorithm to scale to massive collocation points
- Contributions
  - Model: student t / Gaussian mixture power spectrum; covariance via inverse Fourier transform; log-domain weights = Jeffreys prior, sparsity, prunes extra frequencies; spectral mixture kernel, first to realize its benefit for these PDEs
  - Algorithm: grid of collocation + boundary (and/or initial) points, GP finite projection; kernel differentiation for derivatives; product covariance, Kronecker product form, multilinear algebra per dimension; no low rank approximations
  - Result: benchmark PDEs; vs PINN and variants, spectral methods, traditional solvers; relative L_{2} errors \sim 10^{-3} or \sim 10^{-4} or smaller; competitors often fail; better local recovery; learned frequencies match ground-truth; ablation (Section C of Appendix) shows collocation points critical

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Many scientific and engineering problems require us to solve a set of partial differential equations (PDEs). Machine learning (ML) solvers have recently got a lot of attention. Compared to traditional numerical methods, ML solvers don't need complex mesh designs and sophisticated numerical tricks, they are simple to implement, and they can solve inverse problems efficiently and conveniently. The most popular ML solver is the physics-informed neural network (PINN). Consider a PDE of the following general form,

where {\mathcal{F}} is the differential operator, \Omega is the domain, and \partial\Omega is the boundary of the domain. The PINN uses a deep neural network (NN) {\widehat{u}}_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\bf x}) to model the solution u. It samples N_{c} collocation points \{{\bf x}_{c}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{c}} from \Omega and N_{b} points \{{\bf x}_{b}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{b}} from \partial\Omega, and then minimizes a loss,

where L_{b}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{N_{b}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{b}}\left({\widehat{u}}_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\bf x}_{b}^{j})-g({\bf x}_{b}^{j})\right)^{2} is the boundary term that fits the boundary condition, and L_{r}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{N_{c}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{c}}\left({\mathcal{F}}[{\widehat{u}}_{{\bm{\theta}}}]({\bf x}_{c}^{j})-f({\bf x}_{c}^{j})\right)^{2} is the residual term that fits the equation.

The PINN has many success stories, but it often has a hard time solving PDEs whose solutions have high-frequency and multi-scale components. This agrees with the “spectrum bias” that has been observed in NN training. NNs can usually learn the low-frequency information efficiently, but learning the high-frequency knowledge is much harder. To alleviate this, recent work constructs a set of random Fourier features from zero-mean Gaussian distributions, and these random features are fed into the PINN layers for training (see (2)). This is effective, but the performance of the method is unstable, and it is very sensitive to the number and scales of the Gaussian variances, which are hard to choose beforehand.

In this paper, we use a different ML solver framework that is arising, Gaussian processes (GP). We propose GP-HM, a GP solver for High frequency and Multi-scale PDEs. Using the Wiener-Khinchin theorem, we can model the solution directly in the frequency domain and estimate the target frequencies from the covariance function. Then we develop an efficient learning algorithm that scales up to massive collocation points, which are critical for capturing high frequencies. Our major contributions are as follows.

- • Model. We use a mixture of student t or Gaussian distributions to model the power spectrum of the solution, so that the dominant frequencies can be captured flexibly. By the Wiener-Khinchin theorem, we derive the GP covariance function with an inverse Fourier transform, and it contains the component weights and frequency parameters. We show that estimating the weights in the log domain is equivalent to giving each weight a Jeffreys prior. This induces strong sparsity, removes excessive frequency components automatically, and drives the remaining ones toward the ground-truth. So our GP can extract the solution frequencies effectively. The covariance function we get from the Gaussian mixture power spectrum is the known spectral mixture kernel. We are therefore the first to realize its rationale and benefit for solving high-frequency and multi-scale PDEs.

- • Algorithm. For efficient computation, we put all the collocation points and the boundary (and/or initial) points on a grid, and we model the solution values at the grid with the GP finite projection. We get the derivative values in the equation by computing the GP conditional mean via kernel differentiation. Next, we multiply our covariance function at each input dimension, which gives a product covariance. We then derive a Kronecker product form for the covariance and cross-covariance matrices. Using the properties of the Kronecker product and multilinear algebra, we restrict the covariance matrix calculation to each input dimension. This substantially reduces the cost, and we can handle massive collocation points without any low rank approximations.

- • Result. We evaluated GP-HM on several benchmark PDEs with high-frequency and multi-scale solutions. We compared with the standard PINN and several state-of-the-art variants, and with spectral methods, which linearly combine a set of trigonometric bases to estimate the solution. We also compared with several other traditional numerical solvers. In all the cases, GP-HM consistently gets relative L_{2} errors at \sim 10^{-3} or \sim 10^{-4} or even smaller, while the competing ML based approaches often failed and had much larger errors. The visualization of the element-wise prediction error shows that GP-HM also recovers the local solution values much better. We looked at the learned frequency parameters and they match the ground-truth. The ablation study in Section C of Appendix also shows that having enough collocation points is critical to the success, which means our efficient learning method is important.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Scientific and engineering problems often demand that we solve a set of partial differential equations (PDEs). Recently, machine learning (ML) solvers have attracted much attention. Compared to traditional numerical methods, ML solvers do not require complex mesh designs and sophisticated numerical tricks, are simple to implement, and can solve inverse problems efficiently and conveniently. The most popular ML solver is the physics-informed neural network (PINN) [1]. Consider a PDE of the following general form,

where {\mathcal{F}} is the differential operator, \Omega is the domain, and \partial\Omega is the boundary of the domain. To solve the PDE, the PINN uses a deep neural network (NN) {\widehat{u}}_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\bf x}) to model the solution u. It samples N_{c} collocation points \{{\bf x}_{c}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{c}} from \Omega and N_{b} points \{{\bf x}_{b}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{b}} from \partial\Omega, and minimizes a loss,

where L_{b}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{N_{b}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{b}}\left({\widehat{u}}_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\bf x}_{b}^{j})-g({\bf x}_{b}^{j})\right)^{2} is the boundary term to fit the boundary condition, and L_{r}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{N_{c}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{c}}\left({\mathcal{F}}[{\widehat{u}}_{{\bm{\theta}}}]({\bf x}_{c}^{j})-f({\bf x}_{c}^{j})\right)^{2} is the residual term to fit the equation.

Despite many success stories, the PINN often struggles to solve PDEs with high-frequency and multi-scale components in the solutions. This is consistent with the “spectrum bias” observed in NN training [2]: NNs can typically learn low-frequency information efficiently, but grasping high-frequency knowledge is much harder. To alleviate this problem, recent work [3] constructs a set of random Fourier features from zero-mean Gaussian distributions, which are then fed into the PINN layers for training (see (2)). While effective, this method has unstable performance and is highly sensitive to the number and scales of the Gaussian variances, which are difficult to choose beforehand.

In this paper, we resort to an alternative arising ML solver framework, Gaussian processes (GP) [4,5]. We propose GP-HM, a GP solver for High frequency and Multi-scale PDEs. By leveraging the Wiener-Khinchin theorem, we can directly model the solution in the frequency domain and estimate the target frequencies from the covariance function. We then develop an efficient learning algorithm that scales up to massive collocation points, which are critical to capture high frequencies. The major contributions of our work are as follows.

- • Model. To flexibly capture the dominant frequencies, we use a mixture of student t or Gaussian distributions to model the power spectrum of the solution. According to the Wiener-Khinchin theorem, we derive the GP covariance function via inverse Fourier transform, and it contains the component weights and frequency parameters. We show that estimating the weights in the log domain is equivalent to assigning each weight a Jeffreys prior, which induces strong sparsity, automatically removes excessive frequency components, and drives the remaining ones toward the ground-truth. In this way our GP can effectively extract the solution frequencies. Our covariance function derived from the Gaussian mixture power spectrum corresponds to the known spectral mixture kernel, so we are the first to realize its rationale and benefit for solving high-frequency and multi-scale PDEs.

- • Algorithm. To enable efficient computation, we place all the collocation points and the boundary (and/or initial) points on a grid, and model the solution values at the grid with the GP finite projection. To obtain the derivative values in the equation, we compute the GP conditional mean via kernel differentiation. Next, we multiply our covariance function at each input dimension to obtain a product covariance, and derive a Kronecker product form for the covariance and cross-covariance matrices. Using the properties of the Kronecker product and multilinear algebra, we restrict the covariance matrix calculation to each input dimension. This substantially reduces the cost and lets us handle massive collocation points without any low rank approximations.

- • Result. We evaluated GP-HM on several benchmark PDEs that have high-frequency and multi-scale solutions. We compared with the standard PINN and several state-of-the-art variants, with spectral methods [6] that linearly combine a set of trigonometric bases to estimate the solution, and with several other traditional numerical solvers. In all the cases, GP-HM consistently achieves relative L_{2} errors at \sim 10^{-3} or \sim 10^{-4} or even smaller, while the competing ML based approaches often failed and gave much larger errors. The visualization of the element-wise prediction error shows that GP-HM also recovers the local solution values much better. We examined the learned frequency parameters and found that they match the ground-truth. Our ablation study in Section C of Appendix also shows that enough collocation points are critical to the success, implying the importance of our efficient learning method.
